 " Marijuana may be shown to be more dangerous than speed, heroin, alcohol and tobacco, "

(MarijuanaNews note: The Australian prohibitionist government has convened a conference, Drugs Summit 2000, in Sydney, which could have been more honestly called Drug Prohibition 2000. It is clear – as the second article explains – that this conference was not about dealing with Australia’s serious problems with hard drugs, but " yesterday, it became more and more clear that unlike the summit last year, which really did allow for full and frank debate on drug law and rehabilitation philosophy, this event has a rather different objective. Indeed, not only does it begin from a fixed viewpoint - that harm-minimisation approaches should not be tolerated by policy-makers and government.. "

In the first article below bad journalism and quackery are combined in an appalling way. Claims about the effects of marijuana, which have no basis in science, and in fact contradict evidence from peer reviewed studies and very large scale long term studies, are accepted without question. This reporter could have determined whether these extraordinary claims were accepted as proven, which is the standard practice on any other issue.

The doctor worshipfully quoted below has views so extreme that one would think that someone would at least question his claims, but no.

Also, isn’t strange that what is -- at the very most – anecdotal evidence, the observations of one obviously very biased clinician on a highly politicized subject, is accepted as sufficient to justify arresting people, but the observations of huge numbers of patients and clinicians about the therapeutic benefits of cannabis is not sufficient to prevent the arrest of sick and dying people.)

June 14, 2000

letters@theage.fairfax.com.au

By Melissa Fyfe

MARIJUANA LINGERS LONGER, DOCTOR WARNS CASUAL USERS

Thousands of casual marijuana smokers who have a joint on the weekend were unaware that they were affected throughout the rest of the week, a drug expert said yesterday.
(MarijuanaNews note: Statement of " fact? " )

John Anderson, a Sydney doctor, said the chemicals in one marijuana cigarette lasted for weeks, leaving the smoker with greater anxiety, depression, slower reaction time and a " cognitive deficit " that reduced the person's ability to distinguish " relevant from irrelevant material ".

(MarijuanaNews note: Speaking of a person's ability to distinguish " relevant from irrelevant material, " consider the following from the Journal of the American Medical Association about the Pope and Yurgelun-Todd study at McLean Hospital in Massachusetts in which the researchers tested college students who smoked marijuana. It was supposedly a test of marijuana withdrawal, because smokers were not allowed to smoke the day before the tests. This study perfectly addresses the points raised by Anderson. Oddly this study is often cited by prohibitionists to claim that marijuana harms mental function because the marijuana users did slightly worse on one test. However, what the study really showed was --

  1. Memory: " (T)he ability to retain newly learned information after a temporal delay appeared to remain relatively intact in the heavy users….with recall functions per se remaining relatively unaffected. "

  2. Repeating word lists: In the first test (Wisconsin Card Scoring Test) shown on the screen, heavy users got 51.3 correct, and light users got 53.3 correct. In the second test of the same type, heavy users got 55.5 correct and light users got 56.3 correct. Hardly a major difference.

  3. Attention span: " (T)he two groups proved virtually identical. " On another measure of attention, " heavy and light users again showed no significant differences…. "

  4. Neurological damage: The study actually says that the light users who used to be very heavy users " unexpectedly… displayed a much higher Verbal Intelligence Quotient " than did those who had never been heavy smokers. " (N)o differences approaching significance were found on any neuropsychological variable.. " between the former heavy users and those who had never been heavy users. " Thus, these analyses…. weigh tentatively against a C(entral) N(ervous) S(ystem) alteration hypothesis. "

The accompanying JAMA editorial says:

" There is far more extensive, consistent evidence of cognitive deficits associated with heavy use of alcohol relative to marijuana. Most of the cognitive impairments observed ... are not large relative to normal cognitive variability observed among individuals; such impairments would not make a heavy marijuana user " stand out from the crowd. "

Moreover, the results published last year from the Johns Hopkins long-term study of over 1,300 marijuana users actually showed that " heavy " marijuana users had less decline in " cognitive " function than non-users. When there is this kind of evidence contradicting Anderson’s claims, they at least should be mentioned. But that would be journalism and this is prohibitionist propaganda.)

One joint a week, Dr Anderson said, could mean being permanently under the influence of marijuana.

" If you pull a cone, or some a joint, once every week you are under the influence of cannabis constantly, " he said.

Dr Anderson, who researches the effects of marijuana on the brain and helps patients quit the drug, said marijuana " hangs around " in the body more than any other drug because it is absorbed by fat.
(MarijuanaNews note: The only real significance of the fat solubility of marijuana is in urine testing. The amount of THC that is released from the fat cells into the blood stream is not enough to produce any psychological or physical effects.)

Dr Anderson became a passionate advocate against legalising marijuana when he discovered a link between his patients with schizophrenia and Attention Deficit Hyperactivity Disorder, and the use of marijuana.
(MarijuanaNews note: That sentence is really wretched journalism that deals with motivation based on an assumption of " facts " that are contradicted by the evidence. Consider the statement, " Dr. Anderson became a passionate advocate against legalising marijuana when he discovered that marijuana was brought to earth by Martians who are plotting to take over the earth. " )

Dr Anderson was a speaker at yesterday's 2000 Australian Drug Summit.

LESS A WAR ON DRUGS THAN ONE ON HARM REDUCTION

No-one would argue that a vehicle promising to foster reasoned debate on a vexed and complex issue such as drug law reform and drug rehabilitation should not be supported - and applauded.

The laudable objective of Drug Summit 2000 was to provide a further new forum for the exchange of ideas and research that some suggest did not get a full airing at last year's State Government-sponsored Drug Summit.

Certainly, the agenda and list of speakers bode well for delegates interested in hearing first-hand the experience of other nations - and individuals - in the battle against the burgeoning drugs scourge.

But yesterday, it became more and more clear that unlike the summit last year, which really did allow for full and frank debate on drug law and rehabilitation philosophy, this event has a rather different objective.

Indeed, not only does it begin from a fixed viewpoint - that harm-minimisation approaches should not be tolerated by policy-makers and government - but it has a clear, rigid goal in sight: to overturn the State Government's 18-month trial of a medically supervised injecting room.

The truth is - and the media must also take responsibility for this - that the most radical Drug Summit experiment, the heroin injecting room, is the one that has received the most publicity and scrutiny.

But it is one of 400 recommendations of which the great majority, if not all, barring the injecting room, relate to drug prevention and rehabilitation - exactly what this conference is supposed to be about.

The speech of the Swedish speaker, Ms Malou Lindholm, was a case in point, highlighting the current preoccupation with injecting rooms. Ms Lindholm provided a well articulated case for Sweden's gradual move over the past 30 years from a so-called liberal approach to drug laws and treatment to a policy push for a " drug-free " society based on tough measures such as random drug testing of individuals on suspicion of use and compulsory rehabilitation.

She provided an impressive array of statistics, including the vastly reduced incidence of drug use among the young - just 3 per cent of Swedish 15 to 16-year-olds admit to having tried drugs (as against more than 40 per cent in Australia).

At the end of her speech, however, she came to the point. Holding a bagful of syringes, swabs and spoons triumphantly aloft for the TV cameras, she said they were given to her " free " at a needle exchange in Kings Cross. A terrible message to Australia's young, she said, a message that using drugs is " normal ".

" You must say no to heroin injecting room ... What next, the State becomes a heroin dealer? "

But then Ms Lindholm was faced with the latest statistics on the Swedish experience. The European Monitoring Centre for Drugs and Drug Addiction records 250 heroin deaths in Sweden in 1996 among a population of 8.8 million compared with 61 deaths among 15.6 million in the Netherlands, which adopts a harm-minimisation approach including injecting rooms.

Ms Lindholm politely but firmly gave short shrift to that debate.
